114 THIRTY-THIRD REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
February 10, 1916. 
Mr. Joseph W. Harris may be reinstated as fourth assistant examiner in 
the Patent Office, the year limit of eligibility for reinstatement being waivea 
in his case. Mr. Harris is said by the Secretary of the Interior to have proved 
particularly efficient in cases involving metallurgy and electro chemistry during 
his service of nearly six years in the Patent Office, and to have been contin￾uously engaged in prosecuting applications for patents from his resignation on 
April 3, 1912, to the present time, thus having had an experience of nearly 10 
years in patent work. In view of the technical character of the position and 
the experience of Mr. Harris, and his evident qualifications for the position, 
the commission joins with the Secretary of the Interior in recommending an 
Executive order to permit his reinstatement. 
February 11, 1916. 
Mrs. Annie E. Hudson may be appointed to a position in the classified service 
without reference to the civil-service rules. Mrs. Hudson has passed the age at 
which she would be eligible to take the civil-service examination. She is now 
holding a temporary position in the municipal service of the District of Colum￾bia. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this 
order. 
February 11, 1916. 
Mr. Monroe Ryles may be appointed as a messenger at $720 per annum in 
the Federal Trade Commission without reference to the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the chairman of the Federal 
Trade Commission, who states that Mr. Ryles is peculiarly qualified for the 
duties to which it is proposed to assign him. The Civil Service Commission 
does not concur in the recommendation. 
February 11, 1916. 
The temporary appointment of Miss Helen Wrenn as clerk in the Bureau of 
Foreign and Domestic Commerce, Department of Commerce, may be made per￾manent without regard to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon 
recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce, who states that she was cer￾tified for temporary appointment after passing the civil-service examination 
in stenography and typewriting, and that with the exception of a brief period 
she has been serving in the bureau named continuously since April 1, 1915; 
that she is unusually efficient and has shown special aptitude in the per￾formance of the various duties assigned to her; and that it is therefore believed 
that her permanent appointment will prove of very great value to the bureau, 
which is especially in urgent need of competent and trained assistants at this 
time, owing to the extraordinary amount and character of work devolving 
upon it. 
February 21, 1916. 
Executive order No. 2263, of October 26, 1915, authorizing the appointment 
of certain persons who were former employees of the United States Commission 
on Industrial Relations to positions in the competitive classified service without 
reference to the civil-service rules, and amended by Executive order No. 2284, 
of December 14, 1915, is hereby further amended by adding the following 
names: Miss E. M. Green, Mr. Carl Hookstadt. 
February 22, 1916. 
Executive order No. 2306, of February 7, 1916, authorizing the appointment 
of Miss Margaret S. Neate as printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Engraving 
and Printing without certification by the Civil Service Commission, is hereby 
amended to read as follows: Miss Margaret S. Neate may be appointed a 
printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing or as a skilled 
laborer in the Government Printing Office without certification by the Civil 
Service Commission. Miss Neate passed the examination for printer’s assistant 
in January, 1915, but has not been reached for certification. She is the daughter 
of Dr. John S. Neate, who served for 22 years in the United States Army, and 
rendered most valuable service in fighting yellow fever, submitting himself 
for experiment, and died in 1912 from a disease believed to have been brought 
on by his service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secre￾tary of the Treasury. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the 
recommendation.

Mr. Edward Rappholt may be reinstated to the position of letter carrier in 
the post office at New York City without regard to the length of his separation 
from the service. Mr. Rappholt was appointed as substitute letter carrier at 
St. Louis, Mo., January 2, 1902; transferred to New York City post office 
August 10, 1908; to the Atlanta, Ga., post office October 16, 1912; and resigned 
December 8, 1912. He made application for reinstatement in December, 1913. 
His application for reinstatement was referred to the postmaster at New York 
City March 11, 1914, and disapproved. This order is issued upon the recom￾mendation of the Acting Postmaster General in view of the fact that Mr. Rapp￾holt’s record as a letter carrier was good, and that the failure to approve his 
request for reinstatement in the New York City post office at a time when it 
could have been made in accordance with the civil-service rules was due to a 
local rule rather than to a departmental rule or policy. The Civil Service Com￾mission does not concur in the recommendation. 
February 28, 1916. 
Mrs. Annie K. Campbell, a special agent in the Bureau of the Census, may 
be appointed without examination under the civil-service rules to act as private 
secretary to the Director of the Census. The Secretary of Commerce states 
that Mrs. Campbell has had 20 years of practical business experience, is an 
accomplished stenographer and typewriter, and a trained correspondent, and 
that her experience has covered both commercial work and the technical side 
of manufacturing in both domestic and foreign trade. She has been serving 
since April 5, 1915, as a special agent in connection with the census of manu￾factures, and has had experience in that work both in the field and at the central 
office. In securing her permanent services the Secretary of Commerce states 
that he is sure the department will benefit by her very unusual experience and 
by her exceptional ability. In view of these facts and the exception of private 
secretaries allowed by the civil-service rules to certain other heads of bureaus, 
the commission concurs with the Secretary of Commerce in recommending 
the issuance of this order.

VI. ORDERS EXCEPTING PERSONS NAMED FROM THE REQUIRE￾MENTS OF THE RULES. 
November 22, 1919. 
Mr. R. Stone Jackson may be appointed as clerk in the Federal Board for 
Vocational Education, on the basis of his more than 25 years’ experience in the 
Auditor's Office of the Treasury Department and in the Food Administration. 
His services are desired in organizing and carrying on the work of accounting 
and disbursements, falling on the Federal Board for Vocational Education in 
large volumes, because of his experience and valuable knowledge of Government 
accounting. 
The Federal Board for Vocational Education and the Civil Service Commission 
recommend this order. 
December 1, 1919. 
Miss Katherine Peters, of Maryland, now temporarily employed as a typist 
in the Office of the Register of the Treasury, may be appointed to a classied 
position in the Government service without reference to the requirements of the 
civil-service rules. 
December 22, 1919. 
Mr, Edward W. Oyster, a veteran of the Civil War, with many years of service 
in the Government Printing Office and Interior and Treasury Departments, may 
be reinstated in the Federal Board for Vocational Education as supervising 
audit clerk, at $2,000 per annum, the requirement of reinstatement and service 
of six months immediately following in one of the departments in which he was 
formerly employed being waived. 
The Civil Service Commission recommends this action because of the long 
and excellent record of Mr. Oyster in the Government service in a supervisory 
capacity. 
January 16, 1920. 
Mis. Mabel E. Bane may be appointed to a clerical position in the Bureau of 
Mines, Interior Department, without examination under the civil-service rules. 
This order is recommended by the Secretary of the Interior because Mrs. 
Bane is the daughter of a Civil War veteran, whose father and three brothers 
enlisted on the same day, and were all killed except her father; her husband 
was a Spanish-American War veteran. She is dependent upon herself for her 
support and that of a minor child, and has rendered satisfactory service under 
temporary appointment in the Bureau of Mines. She has been unable to pass 
the usual civil-service examination, having failed in several attempts by narrow 
margins. 
The Civil Service Commission does not find sufficient grounds on which to 
base concurrence in recommending this order. 
January 29, 1920. 
Mr. James Hagerman, jr.,, may be appointed as Deputy Commissioner of 
Internal Revenue at $5,000 per annum without examination under the ecivil￾service rules. He is well qualified. The Civil Service Commission, not having 
authority to approve the appointment without competition as requested by the 
department, suggested Executive action. 
February 29, 1920. 
Miss Marian Kearns, of the District of Columbia, may be transferred from the 
position of clerk to sign tribal deeds, $1,200 per annum, office of the Secretary, 
Interior Department, to a regular clerkship. She has served efficiently in the 
Department of the Interior since May 21, 1918, and has demonstrated her 
ability as a clerk. 
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation for an 
Executive order. 
May 10, 1920. 
Mr. Andrew K. Armstrong may be reinstated as chief, section of box tests, 
at $3,240 per annum, forest products laboratory, of the Forest Service, for

Mr. Armstrong served for more than seven years under the Department of 
Agriculture as an engineer of timber tests and assistant engineer in forest prod￾ucts, and his experience since his resignation on December 31, 1917, has been 
along lines increasing his capacity for the successful performance of the duties

May 21, 1920. 
Mrs. Margaret H. Bowen may be appointed to a position in the Postal Service 
without regard to the requirements of the civil-service rules and regulations. 
Mrs. Bowen was temporarily employed in the Washington City post office during 
the period of the late war and performed satisfactory service. This order is 
issued upon the recommendation of the Postmaster General. 
June 19, 1920. 
John KE. Lamiell, formerly post-office inspector, who entered the classified 
service by virtue of a competitive examination, may be reinstated to the position 
of post-office inspector without regard to the year limitation as prescribed by the 
civil-service rules. 
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Postmaster General, in

return to this country and reenter the inspection service of the Post Office 
Department after the Haitien Government had the benefit of his services in 
systematizing and reorganizing its postal service.

April 23, 1915. 
Fred Gilmore, of the District of Columbia, and Robert Taylor, of the District of Columbia, unclassified laborers at $660 per annum in the Post Office Department, may be appointed classified laborers at $660 per annum in the same department without reference to civil-service rules. The above order was issued on request of the Postmaster General, who stated that these men were highly desirable as messengers, entirely trustworthy, and had rendered excellent service, having been directly connected with the office of the Postmaster General since the beginning of the present administration. 
April 27, 1915. 
Mr. Charles W. G. Brett may be transferred from the position of mechanician at 
$1,200 per annum to a clerkship at the same salary, in the Bureau of the Census, Department of Commerce, without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Brett was appointed as mechanician on September 16, 1908. On March 19, 1912, he met with an accident, in the line of duty, which resulted in the loss of his left eye. His transfer to the clerical rollisrecommended by the Director of the Census, who states that Mr. Brett’s experience in connection with the various machines used in the bureau, his familiarity with the matter to be tabulated, and his general educa- tion are believed to be such as to fit him for clerical duties, and that his services have always been satisfactory. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
April 27, 1915. 
Mrs. Lillian B. S. Grant may be reinstated to a position in the classified service in the Post Office Department without regard to the length of time she has been sep- arated from the service. Mrs. Grant, as Mrs. Lillie B. Silcott, was appointed to the position of printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Printing and Engraving on August 2, 1895, and was pro- moted to operative and through the several grades of that position. On July 1, 1902, she was transferred to the Post Office Department as clerk at $900, and was promoted to $1,000 July 1, 1905. She resigned May 9, 1912. 
The Postmaster General advises that it is stated that Mrs. Grant’s husband is a ermanent invalid, and that she is therefore compelled to provide a livelihood for Poth her husband and herself. In view of the circumstances and the fact that the records of the department show that her services were satisfactory and her duties faithfully discharged, the Postmaster General states that no objection would be offered by the department to the reinstatement of Mrs. Grant by Executive order. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of an order in this 
case. 
April 27, 1915. 
Mrs. Lucy Jones Harris, of Kentucky, may be appointed to a position in the Immi- gration Service, Department of Labor, without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued in view of the statement of the Secretary of Labor that the department can use to advantage the services of Mrs. Harris in the Immigration Service, in which the Commissioner General of Immigration informs him there is urgent need 
of a woman of Mrs. Harris’s peculiar qualifications in the labor distribution branch of the service at New York City, where it is deemed advisable, in the development of this new service, to have a woman of her high character and sympathetic initiative, who is able at once to take care of the Teqiiremanis of the woman labor problem and greatly assist in carrying out the plan of distribution inauguarted by the department. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of an order in this case. 
May 4, 1915. 
Mr. William Leroy Fairbanks may be transferred from chief clerk of the American Embassy at London to a clerkship in the Department of Commerce. He has served since 1908, at first in the State Department, then in the American Legation at Peking, and since 1910 in his present position. The Secretary of Commerce, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, recommends the issuance of this order in view of the special qualifications of Mr. Fairbanks for the work of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce. 
May 11, 1915. 
Miss Agnes Deery may be appointed as a nurse in the Indian Service without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. . This action, based upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior, is in fulfillment of

Miss Deery served from June 12, 1902, to May 7, 1914, at the Apache Indian Hos- pital at Fort Sill, Okla., with distinguished faithfulness and success in the positions 
of matron and nurse. The Apache prisoners having been removed to the Mescalero Agency, N. Mex., it is desired to appoint Miss Deery as nurse in the Indian Service. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation for this order. 
May 11, 1915. 
Mrs. Enna Wilson Noel may be reinstated to a position in the classified service in the War Department without regard to the requirements of the civil service rules. Mrs. Noel is the widow of Edward McC. Noel, whose death on April 16, 1915, termi￾nated a service of nearly 33 years in the office of the Surgeon General, and leaves her dependent upon employment for support. Prior to her marriage she served as clerk in the office of the Surgeon General from December 18, 1893, to February 9, 1900, and previously in other offices since November 7, 1889. Her reinstatement is recom- mended by the Secretary of War and the Surgeon General of the Army. The Civil ServicesCommission does not concur in the recommendation. 
May 11, 1915. 
Mrs. Laura F. Richmond may be reinstated as an operative in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been separated from the service. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Acting Secretary of the Treasury in view of the efficient service rendered by the husband of Mrs. Richmond in the Treasury Department for 28 years, and in view of the fact that Mr. Richmond is now wholly incapacitated both mentally and physically for the performance of duty, and also because of the satisfactory service rendered by Mrs. Richmond while a former employee in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing where she served for a period of 
seven years. 
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
May 13, 1915. 
Michael L. Eidsness, jr., of Iowa, a minor clerk of class D ($900) in the Post Office Department, may be promoted to the position of clerk without further civil service examination. 110 REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
MISCELLANEOUS ORDERS. 
PROMOTION TO CLERK POSITIONS, OFFICE OF AUDITOR FOR POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT. 
April 28, 1910. 
Twenty-five positions of clerk, at $900, in the office of the Auditor for the Post Office Department may, as vacancies occur therein, be filled and refilled by promotion on noncompetitive clerk examination from among the employees heretofore transferred from the Bureau of Engraving and Printing who have had seven years of service, at least two years of which shall have been in the office of the Auditor for the Post Office Department. (The order, which is designed to offer to this class of employees some opportunity for advancement as a reward and incentive to faithful work, was recommended by the Secretary of the Treasury and has received the approval of the Civil Service Commission.) ; 
EMPLOYMENT OF ENGINEERS DETAILED BY FRENCH GOVERNMENT. 
May 6, 1910. 
The engineers detailed by the French Government to observe certain public works in the United States may be employed as junior engineers in the Engineer Department at Large, without examination under civil-service rules. 
The employment contemplated was temporary in character and its aim was to 
present an opportunity to young engineers to familiarize themselves with the work 
by being permitted to assist in its construction and become professionally responsible 
for its execution. As the law prohibits the acceptance of gratuitous services, it was 
necessary in order to comply with the wishes of the French Government to make 
them employees, their compensation being only nominal. 
POSITION OF EDITOR, BUREAU OF EDUCATION, TO BE FILLED WITHOUT EXAMINATION. 
July 1, 1910. 
The present vacancy in the position of editor in the Bureau of Education may be filled by appointment without regard to the requirement of examination. This action is taken on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior and the Civil Service Commission in view of the failure of two civil-service examinations to secure eligibles with the required qualifications of a broad general education, familiarity with the educational literature of the United States and foreign countries, acquaintance with educational leaders, ability to do good report writing and to address educational gatherings, and good judgment in the examination of manuscripts sub- mitted with a view to publication. 
RETENTION OF DISTRICT AGENTS AND ASSISTANT DISTRICT AGENTS, INDIAN SERVICE. 
July 12, 1910. 
Those persons who were employed on June 30, 1910, or within the year preceding, as district agents and assistant district agents (local representatives of the Secretary of the Interior in Oklahoma), and who are certified by the Secretary of the Interior as competent and efficient may be retained, but shall not by such retention obtain a competitive status; and all vacancies which may occur in said positions shall be filled - by the transfer of persons properly serving in the Indian Service under the Com- missioner to the Five Civilized Tribes or in the Union Agency. It was at first thought that the demand for the services of these employees would be temporary, but when it was found that the work would be likely to continue for several years it was deemed advisable by the Interior Department and the Civil Service Commission to make provision for the retention of those employees’ services who have been found competent and efficient and to provide for filling future vacancies by transfer. 
CLASSIFICATION OF ASSISTANT POSTMASTERS, AND OF CLERKS IN CERTAIN FIRST AND 
SECOND CLASS POST OFFICES. 
September 30, 1910. 
It is hereby ordered that the position of assistant postmaster in post offices of the first and second classes and also the position of clerk of whatever grade in post offices 
of the first and second classes not hitherto classified shall be included in the classified
next_page_text:
REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE cOMMISSION. 111 
competitive service, provided that no assistant postmaster or clerk appointed with- out examination prior to this order shall be classified who fails to establish to the satisfaction of the Post Office Department his capacity for efficient service in the position held, and Schedule A of the Civil Service Rules is hereby amended accord- ingly; this order to take effect December 1, 1910. 
AUTHORITY TO COMMISSION TO EXCEPT POSITIONS OF UNUSUAL CHARACTER. 
December 1, 1910. 
The Civil Service Commission is hereby authorized to except from competitive examination, as contemplated by the civil-service act, section 2, clause Second, subject to the limitations prescribed by the statute and those now set forth in Rule II, certain positions arising, of unusual character, as to duties, and for which qualified persons are so rare that, in the judgment of the commission, they can not, in the interests of good civil-service administration, be filled through open competitive examination. In every instance of the exercise of this power the same procedure shall be followed as required in the Executive order of November 22, 1907. 
TRANSFER OF FURLOUGHED EMPLOYEES, RESIDENTS OF STATES IN EXCESS UNDER THE 
APPORTIONMENT. 
December 20, 1910. 
The Secretary of Commerce and Labor has reported to me that in carrying out the plan of reorganization of the Lighthouse Service, it became necessary to place on fur- lough without pay a number of employees whose records were entirely satisfactory. The Secretary reports, further, that announcement was made that the furloughed employees would be considered for transfer to other branches of the service of the Department of Commerce and Labor whenever vacancies occurred. EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 
General Executive orders and special exceptions to the civil-service rules from September 15, 1915, to August 31, 1916, are published in the Thirty-third Annual Report. The following are general orders and special exceptions from September 1, 1916, to October 1, 1917: 
I. GENERAL ORDERS AMENDING THE CIVIL SERVICE RULES.

August 6, 1913. 
Mr. Thomas H. Vanderford may be reinstated to an appropriate position in the Internal Revenue Service without reference to the period of his separation from the service. 
Mr. Vanderford was a deputy collector of internal revenue from October 11, 1893, to July 10, 1898, when he was removed for political reasons. A former collector of internal revenue, under whom he served and by whom he was separated from the service, makes the following statement regarding him in a letter dated May 9, 1913: “Mr. Vanderford was an officer in the service when I was appointed collector in 
1898 and had been for four years prior to my appointment. He served under me for practically a year. I regarded him as one of the best officers in the service and after 10 years’ experience as collector I think I can truthfully say he was as good an officer as I ever knew. I separated him from the service in order to appoint a man of my own party.” The Commissioner of Internal Revenue in a letter dated July 7, 1913, states that he has personally “known Mr. Vanderford for many years, that he is a man of sterling integrity, honest and fearless, and in his opinion possesses just such traits of character as would make a competent and efficient revenue officer. The records of the Internal Bevoune Bureau show that he rendered satisfactory service and was an efficient employee. 
In view of the above facts the commission concurs with the recommendation of the Sag of the Treasury and the Commissioner of Internal Revenue for the issuance of this order. 
August 9, 1913. 
Miss Sarah A. Prender, who is now serving as a skilled laborer in the Post Office Department, may be appointed to a clerical position not higher than class E on the permanent roll of that department without regard to the civil-service act. 
August 20, 1913. 
Mr. Charles M. McCabe may be reinstated as a clerk in the Postal Service without reference to the year limitation of the reinstatement rule. Mr. McCabe was removed from the Nashville, Tenn., post, office on September 10, 1898, notice of his removal alleging ‘‘inefficiency.”” No charge of inefficiency had been preferred against him and he was allowed no opportunity to reply to the charge as required by the rules then in effect. Mr. McCabe as a member of the board of civil service examiners for the Nashville post office rendered assistance to the commission in connection with investigations involving the collector of internal revenue, who was removed by the President for violation of the civil service rules. The Postmaster General states that it appears that Mr. McCabe was removed on political grounds, and the issuance of an Executive order for his reinstaterient seems to be justified by the facts in the case. In view of the facts stated above the Civil Service Commission concurs in recom- mending this order. 
August 25, 1913. 
Section 3 of the Regulations Governing Appointments to the Navy-Yard Service is hereby waived so as to permit of the appointment of Pedro Abrain to the position of 
general helper at $2.32 per diem at the navy yard, Mare Island, Cal. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy and is based upon the fact that Abrain was injured in the line of duty as a fireman on board the U. S. 8. Prometheus and is unable to perform the duties of a fireman. 
August 25, 1913. 
Section 3 of the Regulations Governing Appointments to the Navy-Yard Service is hereby waived so as to permit of the Sppeinishens of Edmond Pawellik to the position 
of general helper at $1.76 per diem at the navy yard, Norfolk, Va. This order 1s issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy and is based upon the fact that Pawellik was discharged from the Navy owing to injuries received in the line of duty and is unable to obtain civil employment. 
September 4, 1913. 
Mr. Pat O'Keefe may be appointed a deputy collector of internal revenue without examination under the civil-service rules. The commission was not consulted regarding this appointment. The reasons stated for the order are that Mr. O’ Keefe possesses excellent qualifications for work of this character, particularly in view of the income-tax provisions of the new tariff bill, and it was desirable that the collector of internal revenue for the State of Texas, where Mr. 0’ Keefe resides, should hava on his staff a man of Mr, O’ Keefe’s peculiar qualifications,

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 131 
September 11, 1913. 
Mr. James D. Scott may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service, without regard to the length of time he has been out of the service. The Postmaster General reports that he was appointed a railway mail clerk on October 17, 1900, at $800 per annum, and promoted through the successive grades until he received a salary of $1,100 per annum; that he resigned voluntarily, April 17,1911; that his record as a clerk is good, and his reinstatement would be to the benefit of the service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending that an Executive order be issued in this case. 
September 17, 1913. 
Miss Emily W. Matter, of the District of Columbia, now temporarily employed in 
the same position through certification by the Civil Service Commission, may be appointed permanently to the position of clerk at $720 per annum in the Coast and 
Geodetic Survey. : The department in recommending this action stated that Miss Matter had demon- strated her fitness during temporary appointment, that the department had been 
unable to make selection from six certifications because of declinations and of the fact that many of the eligibles were found unsuitable. 
September 17, 1913. 
Mrs. Annie S. Renick, of the District of Columbia, may be appointed to the position of clerk at $1,000 per annum in the Department of State, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. 
September 18, 1913. 
Mr. William B. Green may be reinstated as a compositor in the Weather Bureau without reference to the time limit imposed by the civil-service rules. 
Mr. Green’s services as a compositor were terminated on December 31, 1910, after more than 20 years’ service. The reason given at the time was that a reduction of the force was necessary because of the transfer of certain work from the Weather Bureau to the Government Printing Office. The Secretary of Agriculture with the concur- rence of the Civil Service Commission recommends the reinstatement because there is reason to believe that Mr. Green was unfairly dealt with because of certain testimony he had given in a case which resulted in the reprimand of the Chief of the Weather Bureau. 
September 18, 1913. 
Mr. David A. Robbins, formerly a letter carrier at Boston, Mass., may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the Postal Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service.

294 EIGHTEENTH EEPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION.
March 16, 1900.
AMENDMENT TO RULE X.
Rule X, section 4, is hereby amended by striking out the proviso thereof and
substituting therefor the following:
Provided, That a person holding a position which is excepted, but which he was
holding at the time of its classification, or which he entered in accordance with the
provisions of these rules at a time when said position was subject to competitive
examination, and has since served continuously therein, or a person holding a
position which is excepted, but which he entered prior to the President’s order of
November 2, 1894, and has since served continuously therein, may, subject to the
other conditions and provisions of this rule, be transferred to a position not excepted.
The section as amended shall read as follows:
4. Transfer shall not be made from an excepted position to a position not excepted:
Provided, That a person holding a position which is excepted, but which he was
holding at the time of its classification, or which he entered in accordance with the
provisions of these rules at a time when said position was subject to competitive
examination, and has since served continuously therein, or a person holding a posi¬
tion which is excepted, but which he entered prior to the President’s order of No¬
vember 2, 1894, and has since served continuously therein, may, subject to the other
conditions and provisions of this rule, be transferred to a position not excepted.
Approved.
Executive Mansion, March 16, 1900.
William McKinley.
AMENDMENT TO RULE X.
Rule X, section 5, is hereby amended by striking out after the word “entered,”
in the third line thereof, the language ‘ ‘ a position appointment to which is made by
the President by and with the advice and consent of the Senate,” and substituting
therefor the following: “an unclassified position in any part of the executive civil
service other than a position of mere laborer or workman, or to serve under the
authority of the General Government as a civilian in the insular possessions under
the control of the United States.”
The section as amended shall read as follows:
5. Transfer shall not be made from a position not classified under the civil-service
act to a classified position: Provided, That a person who, by promotion or transfer
from a classified position, has entered an unclassified position in any part of the
executive civil service other than a position of mere laborer or workman, or to serve
under the authority of the General Government as a civilian in the insular posses¬
sions under the control of the United States, and has served continuously therein
from the date of said promotion or transfer, may be transferred from said unclassified
position to the position from wdiich he was so transferred, or to any position to which
transfer could be made therefrom.
Approved.
William McKinley.
Executive Mansion, March 16, 1900.

limitations and confine competition in examinations for such positions to persons
within such limitations.
